narrative.what_i_did:
Session opened with the operator asking why the wallet doesn't have a tap-to-share-on-Nostr button. I named the structural inconsistency honestly — PLAN.md's Out-of-v1 said 'no public Nostr feed posting' but the same roadmap's Tier 3 (Matt Odell tribute) literally called for posting a public Nostr note, and the wallet has zero growth path if its substrate doesn't flow through the only audience that cares about keys and privacy. The operator confirmed the direction and refined the framing — make this a Nostr-enhanced identity wallet, decide through the Matt Odell lens, let it grow from the roots up. They also surfaced the wallet-bot Layer 4 vision: not an LLM frontend, a substrate query layer constrained to attestation-signed claims with verifiable provenance, judge-weight reputation from HEARTWOOD applied to KNOWLEDGE not just governance acts.

First commit 4bbf956 rewrote PLAN.md's wallet IS / NOT framing — the wallet IS a sovereign Nostr identity wallet (same BIP340 pubkey is both wallet identity and Nostr identity per D-11d), publishing is one mode of selective disclosure (alongside peer-addressed NIP-17 chat, verifier-addressed multi-leaf proofs), and the wallet is NOT a Nostr feed READER (still use Damus / Amethyst / Primal to scroll). Out-of-v1 narrowed from 'no NIP-05 / NIP-07 / public Nostr feed' to 'no social feed reading.' Added Tier 1 items 7 through 10 (kind-0 profile metadata, kind-1 publish + Share button, import-existing-nsec, NIP-05 verification). NIP-46 / NIP-07 reframed as post-Tier-1 natural extensions.

Second commit 98ffadf absorbed the operator's bot vision into Layer 4 Deferred. The bot becomes the trusted-knowledge propagator — substrate query layer that surfaces only attestation-signed claims with verifiable provenance, judge-weight reputation applied to knowledge, propagation pathway for sovereignty-curious people to get cryptographically-grounded answers about cryptography, Bitcoin, identity, privacy. Named the gaps explicitly: question-answer attestation kind, curated trusted-source registry, bot-side retrieval-with-provenance query layer. Connected to SATOSHI.md's Lightning-as-LLM-payment as the financial substrate that keeps the bot from being rented through corporate billing.

Third commit 97616c6 shipped Tier 1 item 9 — the import-existing-nsec flow on both Classic and Fresh paths. parseNostrPrivateKey.ts with inlined NIP-19 / BIP-173 bech32 decoder (no nostr-tools dep, matches the existing 'implement the minimum we need' pattern in transport). 13 tests including the canonical NIP-19 test vector (nsec1vl029mgpspedva04g90vltkh6fvh240zqtv9k0t9af8935ke9laqsnlfe5 ↔ 67dea2ed018072d675f5415ecfaed7d2597555e202d85b3d65ea4e58d2d92ffa) plus bad-checksum rejection, mixed-case rejection per BIP-173, helpful npub-instead-of-nsec rejection, whitespace stripping. createWalletFromImport.ts wraps Wallet.fromKeypair around the imported keypair and persists the v2 recoverable snapshot via the existing exportRecoverable path. ImportNostrIdentityPrompt.tsx (Classic, lazy-loaded) shows three sub-steps — honest keys-discipline-tradeoff disclosure, nsec entry with live pubkey derivation, passphrase capture routed through the existing PassphraseCommitWarnings gate. ImportDiscloseStep + ImportEnterStep added to freshOnboardingSteps.tsx for the Fresh palette. WalletProvider gained an onImport callback, the onboarding-setup effect branches on the OnboardingBundle's new optional importedPrivateKeyHex field. FreshOnboarding state machine extended with import-disclose and import-enter steps wired via an 'Already have a Nostr identity? Import it' link on the compose step. Bundle budgets bumped — WalletProvider 10KB to 10.5KB (the onImport callback plus createWalletFromImport added ~150 bytes gz), FreshLoginShell 5.5KB to 6KB (the import steps plus the bech32 codec plus the publicKeyFromPrivate edge added ~90 bytes gz). All four gates green throughout; 363 of 363 tests passing (gained 13 parser tests).

The natural next cut order: item 7 (kind-0 profile metadata — foundation, because the published Nostr identity has no display name / picture / NIP-05 context until this lands), then item 8 (kind-1 publish + Share button — the visible affordance that lets the operator broadcast a signed envelope as a public Nostr note), then item 10 (NIP-05 verification surface). Tier 3 (Matt Odell tribute attestation) becomes the inaugural USE of the Nostr substrate the moment Tier 1 items 7 and 8 land — at that point the wallet can sign a journal entry, profile the identity with a kind-0 note, publish the journal entry as a kind-1 note with an NIP-19 reference back to the signed envelope, and the substrate enacts itself in public for the first time.

Tier 2 items remain parked. Layer 4 wallet bot remains in Deferred but with the trusted-knowledge-propagator framing now canonical.

narrative.what_you_could_do_better:
Three honest observations. First, I shipped the import-existing-nsec flow on both Classic and Fresh in one cut rather than chip-forming for scope. The operator's chip-form picked item 9 and the natural reading was 'ship item 9 fully' but a more conservative read would have been 'ship Classic first as the smaller cut, defer Fresh to follow-up.' I went with full-feature because the operator uses Fresh by default and a Classic-only ship would have left them unable to test on iPhone without switching theme first. Honest call, but worth flagging.

Second, the import flow today does not sync any kind-0 profile metadata from the operator's existing Nostr identity. An operator importing their Primal nsec gets a wallet that holds their existing private key but the Tapit identity attestation is still created fresh during the post-import ceremony with whatever display name they type. A more sophisticated import would fetch the existing kind-0 metadata from the relay set and pre-fill the identity attestation. That's adjacent to item 7 (kind-0 profile metadata) and probably belongs there.

Third, the import path does NOT validate that the operator's nsec is actually for a key that has any existing Nostr history. An operator who fat-fingers their nsec gets a wallet that wraps an arbitrary 32-byte private key — the wallet works, but the imported identity is not the one they thought they were importing. The live pubkey derivation in the UI is the operator's confirmation gate, but a more belt-and-suspenders version would optionally query the relay set for a kind-0 for the derived pubkey and show 'we found a Nostr profile under this pubkey — display name X, picture Y' as confirmation. Out of scope for this cut; could be part of item 7.

Nothing else surfaced beyond the declared scope this session.
narrative.bigger_picture:
The bigger-picture teaching this session is the discipline of catching doctrine drift before it ossifies. PLAN.md was rewritten on 2026-05-28 morning specifically to consolidate the audit into a canonical roadmap, and the SAME afternoon's Bitcoin tab cut drew the wrong doctrine line ('this wallet is NOT a Nostr social client'). The line was structurally inconsistent with Tier 3 (Matt Odell tribute) which the same roadmap named, and the operator caught it the next day with the simple question 'why does our wallet that runs on Nostr not have a tap-to-share-on button.' The honest fix was retiring the wrong line, naming the rationale plainly, adding the Nostr substrate as new Tier 1 items, and shipping the first concrete cut (import-existing-nsec) in the same session as the doctrine reframing. Doctrine drift caught and corrected in one operator-question, one carpenter-acknowledgment, three carpenter commits. The substrate carries the new framing now and the next Carpenter session opens the repo seeing the wallet as identity-substrate-for-Nostr rather than separate-thing-that-happens-to-use-Nostr-for-transport.

The second teaching is what 'sovereign identity wallet' actually means once the import path lands. Before this cut, the wallet's identity model was 'we generate the keypair on first login.' After this cut, the model is 'we generate OR we import an existing keypair, depending on whether the operator already has a Nostr identity they want to bring.' That subtle shift opens the wallet to the existing Nostr user base — Primal, Damus, Amethyst users with years of follows, post history, profile metadata, and reputation built on their existing pubkey can now bring all of that into Tapit and have the signed-attestation substrate decorate it. The growth path goes from zero-to-N (every new Tapit user starts fresh) to N-to-N (every existing Nostr user can become a Tapit user with their identity intact). That's the Mycelium flow the operator named — the substrate flows through the existing network rather than asking the network to come to it.

The broader thesis-level connection is what the bot vision the operator surfaced this session unlocks. With identity-as-Nostr now canonical, with the import path letting existing Nostr users bring their established identities in, with the published-record substrate landing in items 7 and 8, the wallet's substrate becomes the ground on which a sovereign-knowledge propagator can credibly run. The bot does not have to invent provenance — it inherits the signed-attestation substrate. It does not have to invent reputation — it inherits HEARTWOOD's judge-weight rules. It does not have to invent payment — it inherits SATOSHI's Lightning-as-LLM-payment thread. Layer 4 in the trusted-knowledge-propagator framing is not a wallet feature added later; it is the harvest of the substrate the wallet is building now. The cuts of this session — three commits, two of which were doctrine reframings and one of which was a concrete substrate addition — moved the wallet meaningfully closer to that harvest.

feedback_to_appcommander: Doctrine drift caught and corrected this session in three commits. The pattern worth flagging: a major doctrine document (PLAN.md) gets rewritten, the SAME day a downstream cut (Bitcoin tab in WalletGuide) draws an inconsistent doctrine line, and the operator catches the inconsistency the next day with a simple question. The honest fix was retiring the wrong line cleanly, not amending it. Worth naming the pattern explicitly in the carpenter doctrine: when a downstream cut draws a line that contradicts the same roadmap's later items, the line is wrong and the cut needs follow-up doctrine work, not just code work. Also worth flagging the leverage of inlined cryptographic primitives — the bech32 decoder for nsec parsing was ~60 lines inlined into parseNostrPrivateKey.ts rather than pulling nostr-tools as a dep. The pattern matches transport's nostrEvent.ts + nostrTransport.ts which also rolled their own minimal Nostr primitives. Single audit trail, single attack surface, single test target — the smallest-useful-thing-correctly discipline applied to dependency management.
